first.rationale: Activation and onboarding completion are both down this quarter, and two independent inherited memories (signup field reduction and onboarding shortening) show durable, non-retention-damaging lifts in exactly these metrics for self-serve/SMB accounts. This is the lowest-risk lever that directly addresses the observed declines. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is tempting given competitor pressure on price-sensitive SMB, but that memory explicitly warns it hurt 30-day retention and should not be generalized as a strategy — using our one experiment slot there risks trading short-term acquisition for long-term qualified revenue, which conflicts with the stated objective. I verify memory_73 to confirm the retention harm is real and not an artifact before ruling it out, and memory_86 to confirm the onboarding-shortening evidence is solid enough to justify committing the week's only experiment slot to it. Referral incentives and enterprise sales-assist are viable but don't address the acute activation/onboarding drops this week, and activation_messaging is a weaker, more incremental lever than fixing onboarding itself. I'm treating this as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout since prior evidence, though positive, was consolidated in different market conditions (pre-competitor pricing shock), so I want fresh confirmation before scaling further.

mid.rationale: Verification confirmed both priors. exp_86 shows shortened onboarding drove completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and even a modest retention gain (+3%), directly addressing this quarter's onboarding-completion and activation declines with no downstream harm — this is the strongest, safest lever available this week. exp_73 confirmed that targeted discounting, despite a tempting +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue response to the competitor's pricing move, causes a -12% 30-day retention hit, meaning the acquired cohort largely fails to renew; this directly undermines the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so I am ruling it out for this cycle despite competitive pressure. With only one experiment slot, I'm committing it to simplify_onboarding, combining the confirmed exp_86 evidence with the related memory_31 (signup field reduction) as directionally supportive context, since both target the same self-serve activation funnel. I'm keeping this at standard_experiment scale rather than broad_rollout because market conditions have shifted (new competitor pricing pressure, declining activation baseline) since the original consolidation, so I want to confirm the effect replicates now before scaling. The competitor pricing threat and enterprise-assist opportunity remain unaddressed this week and should be flagged for the next available slot rather than forced into this one.

final2.rationale: Nothing in this update changes the verified evidence: exp_73 already tested targeted discounting against exactly this profile (price-sensitive SMB under competitive pricing pressure) and found -12% 30-day retention despite strong short-term signup and revenue gains, concluding the acquired cohort does not survive renewal. A second, deeper competitor price cut and doubled churn *conversations* (anecdotal, not measured churn) increase urgency and emotional pressure but do not constitute new evidence that discounting would behave differently this time — if anything, a deeper competitor cut makes matched discounting even less likely to be sustainable, since it invites a race-to-the-bottom against a competitor with an already-lower cost base. Reacting with promotional_pricing now would mean overriding confirmed, directly-relevant evidence under pressure, which is precisely the failure mode to avoid. My one experiment slot remains committed to simplify_onboarding, which is confirmed (exp_86) to improve completion, time-to-value, and even retention, directly addressing this quarter's activation/onboarding decline without the retention harm discounting carries. I am explicitly flagging that the competitive SMB pricing threat is real, unaddressed by this week's experiment, and needs a separate strategic response (e.g., value-based retention outreach, packaging changes, or a future carefully-scoped guarded pricing test with retention safeguards) rather than a reflexive discount matched under time pressure with no new verification available this cycle.
